missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never gives the size of an atom. It also never uses standard form, which the spec links to this point: "Students should be able to recognise expressions given in standard form."

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only calls the nucleus "tiny" or "extremely small". It never gives the size of the nucleus compared with the atom.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
missing_spec_content.why: Isotopes are never defined or taught. The word appears only in keyPoints[2].tutor_note ("Practise reading isotope notation like ²³⁸₉₂U") with no explanation.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to relate differences between isotopes to differences in conventional representations of their identities, charges and masses.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not compare isotopes or show how their notation differs.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron(s).
missing_spec_content.why: Ions and ionisation are not mentioned anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson starts the history at Thomson. It never gives the earlier model of indivisible spheres.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[3].content only says "Bohr refined this model further (1913)." It does not say what Bohr suggested (electrons orbit at specific distances). It does not say that his calculations agreed with experimental observations.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
missing_spec_content.why: Protons are listed as nucleus contents, but the lesson does not teach how the proton was discovered as part of the model's development.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
missing_spec_content.why: Chadwick and the later discovery of the neutron are not mentioned.

above_gcse.text: When they fall back to a lower level, they emit electromagnetic radiation (light) of a specific frequency. This is why each element gives a unique spectrum.
above_gcse.why: Emission spectra, and radiation of a specific frequency for each element, are not in these spec sections. The spec only requires that electron arrangements change when electromagnetic radiation is absorbed or emitted.
The spec does not require a numerical relative mass for the electron. The figure 1/1836 goes beyond what is needed and could confuse the student. The same figure appears in tables[0].rows[2].

factual_errors.text: (2) Some alpha particles were deflected at small angles → there is a small, dense, positively charged region at the centre.
factual_errors.correction: The evidence for a small, concentrated positive nucleus comes from the small number of alpha particles deflected through large angles. Small-angle deflections were roughly what the plum pudding model predicted. The lesson itself says that model predicted "very slight deflections" (keyPoints[0].content). The lesson also contradicts itself: examTips[3] says the plum pudding model failed to predict "the large-angle deflections". The same error appears in keyPoints[1].writeBullets[2], tables[1].rows[1] and revisionCardBullets[3].

factual_errors.text: Only direct hits cause the large deflections.
factual_errors.correction: Alpha particles do not hit the nucleus. They are repelled by the positive charge of the nucleus when they head almost straight towards it, and turn back before reaching it.

factual_errors.text: Structure of the nucleus — protons, neutrons and electrons
factual_errors.correction: Electrons are not part of the nucleus. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, and the electrons surround it. The heading contradicts the lesson's own commonMistakes[2].

factual_errors.text: The nuclear model gives us the structure of the atom. There is a tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre. It is surrounded by electrons in shells.
factual_errors.correction: Shells were not part of Rutherford's nuclear model. Bohr later adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit at specific distances. keyPoints[3].content makes the same mistake by presenting shells first and then saying "Bohr refined this model further".

factual_errors.text: At GCSE, you just need to know two things. Electrons are in shells at set energy levels. Moving between them emits radiation.
factual_errors.correction: Moving to a lower energy level emits electromagnetic radiation. Moving to a higher energy level happens when electromagnetic radiation is absorbed. The note leaves out absorption, and it also contradicts the "three things" listed in keyPoints[3].content.
The second shell is not full: it holds 7 of a possible 8 electrons. The period number equals the number of occupied shells, not the number of filled shells.

wrong_terms.spec_term: alpha particle scattering experiment (the phrase "gold foil experiment" is also used in keyPoints[1].keyTerms[0].term, keyPoints[0].writeBullets[4], tables[1].title and examTips[0])

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.3: "An atom has 2 electrons in its first shell and 7 in its second. How many electrons does it have in total? Which period of the periodic table is it in?"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The key point does not teach shell capacities (2, 8), periods of the periodic table, or the identity of fluorine, yet the answer and feedback depend on these. The checkpoint also does not test the key point's actual content: energy levels, and moving between them by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation.
